utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, ladies and gentlemen; good morning, interpreters. Can they hear me? Yes, they can. Good morning to the technicians; good morning, counsel for the Prosecution. As far as I can see, Mr. McCloskey is not here. Good morning to the counsel for the Defence. Good morning, General Krstic. We will be sitting in full composition today, together with Judge Wald, and we will continue with hearing the Krstic case. Good morning, Colonel Kingori. I hope you have spent a nice weekend here in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was a nice weekend. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. Let me just remind you that you are still under an oath and that you are going to continue answering questions that will be put to you by Mr. Cayley -- no, I'm sorry, Mr. Harmon. Mr. Harmon, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours; good morning, counsel; good morning, Colonel Kingori.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When we concluded your testimony on Friday, you were discussing events, particularly focusing on events in Potocari on the 12th and the 13th of July. Let me ask you, Colonel Kingori, on the 12th of July, you were wearing a pair of sunglasses, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did something happen in respect of your sunglasses, and can you explain to the Judges what did occur?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, on that day, when I was still patrolling just around where the refugees were, one of the BSA soldiers intercepted me and asked me whether he could have my sunglasses. Okay. The way he asked me was not that polite --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm getting the French translation, at least I have. I'm getting a perfect French translation. Could we hear from the English booth, if possible?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can you hear us now?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your answer, Colonel Kingori?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, on that day, while I was still patrolling that area, that is, where the refugees were, one of the BSA soldiers confronted me and requested to have my sunglasses. Actually, it was not a request, he wanted to remove them. Luckily, one of the senior officers, and that member was Colonel-- the legal officer, the one who introduced himself as the legal officer, intercepted and told that guy to leave me alone. So at least I had my sunglasses back.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Have I shown you some video footage and have you been able to identify the soldier who you believe was responsible for attempting to take your sunglasses?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you have done, and I can recognise him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If I could have the lights dimmed please, and if we could play Prosecutor's Exhibit 76, I would like you to identify the soldier who you believe was responsible for trying to take your sunglasses, please.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What is he wearing?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one I'm pointing at, he's wearing a jacket. I can't remember which colour that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Would you replay that, please? Freeze it.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This one here, he has a T-shirt, he has a pistol, some -- here he is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The man in the centre of this particular frame.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's fine, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Colonel Kingori, did BSA soldiers who were in Potocari on the 12th and 13th take items from UNPROFOR soldiers while you were there?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this was an ongoing thing. They could take belongings from the DutchBat soldiers, who were members of UNPROFOR, and also from the civilians who were there. That was an ongoing thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, let me change the topic and ask you if, on the 13th of July, you saw Major Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 13th of July, Your Honour, I saw him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Where did you see him?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was there almost throughout, but at least I remember seeing him inside the DutchBat compound and also outside the DutchBat compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: What do you remember him doing on the 13th of July in the DutchBat compound?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the DutchBat compound, he came there to check those refugees who were still inside there, that is, the ones who were injured, the ones who were actually sick, to check whether there were any soldiers, and he had a list that he was comparing with, which I believe was that of the soldiers that he knew belonged to the BiH, and he was cross-checking. Whichever male that he found, he could cross-check with their list to see whether he belonged to the BiH or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And how long did he remain in the UN compound, as far as you can recall?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, he stood there for quite some time, quite some time, actually, maybe close to one hour, something like that. And he was not alone, he was together with some other senior BSA officers. He was with Colonel Acamovic, he was with -- okay, Petar, that is, our interpreter, and Vukovic was also there that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me ask you, you mentioned the name that's new here to us, Acamovic. Who was Colonel Acamovic?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, Colonel Acamovic was introduced to us as a logistics officer, and also later on he told us that he was the special representative of General Mladic in that particular area.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And was that -- when you had those comments made by Colonel Acamovic, do you remember what day that was? Was that the 12th or the 13th or some other day?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, here I'm not very sure, but I think it was on the 13th. I'm not very sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Now, let me ask you, in your testimony on Friday, you discussed seeing General Krstic and other high-ranking officers of the Bosnian Serb army on the 12th of July, and you saw them in Potocari. I'm going to play you two clips of film, and I've had an opportunity to show you these clips of film, have I not? These are interviews, the first interview with General Mladic and the second is an interview with General Krstic. Did you have an opportunity to see those films?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have. You have shown me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And did I show you those films for the first time on Friday night, after you concluded your testimony?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Now, if I could pass out to the Chamber and to counsel a transcript, which would be Prosecutor's Exhibit 79A, that's the English version, and 79B, the B/C/S version, before we play this film, it would assist the Chamber and counsel in understanding what's on the film.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Before we play this film, Colonel Kingori, do you appear in this film, in the interview of General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And, in fact, you appear at the very beginning of this film, do you not?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Then if we could lower the lights, please, and if we could then play Prosecutor's Exhibit 79, we could hear the interview of General Mladic

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Colonel Kingori, you were present when that interview took place, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you remember which day that was? Was that the 12th or the 13th?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That should have been on the 12th.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me now play a second tape for you, a taped interview of General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And before I play that tape, I'd also ask the usher to disseminate Prosecutor's Exhibit 67A and B, which is an English and B/C/S transcript of the tape. Now, if we could proceed by playing Prosecutor's Exhibit 66. Lower the lights, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Colonel Kingori, if I could first of all ask you, can you tell, from looking at that film, where that film was taken?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can. I can remember it was -- even from the buildings which are there, I can be able to tell that it was somewhere ahead of Potocari, as you go towards Srebrenica. It is somewhere near those factories which were there. I can recall that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, you didn't actually see that interview take place, did you?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Friday in your testimony, you identified a number of people who you saw in Potocari, and you identified a particular individual, I'm going to have the usher place the photograph on the ELMO, an individual you saw who was present with General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And if I could have placed on the ELMO Prosecutor's Exhibit 28/8.1.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Again, Judge Wald was not here, Colonel Kingori. Can you identify with your pointer the man you saw with General Krstic in Potocari in this photograph?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the man [indicates].

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Indicating, for the record, the man in the brown T-shirt on the left side of the image. Now, if we could go back to the film, to the portion of General Krstic's interview, the portion that I have previously asked to be freeze-framed, and if I could direct Your Honours' attention to the video monitor.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'd like to direct, Colonel Kingori, your attention first to the man who appears over the left-hand shoulder of General Krstic, and I'd like to direct Your Honours' attention to that individual as well. You can see him in the background. He's walking from the right-hand side of the monitor to the left, in the direction of General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Usher, if you would kindly take Prosecutor's Exhibit 58, and if that could be disseminated to the Judges, and if you could place Prosecutor's Exhibit 58 on the ELMO next to Prosecutor's Exhibit 28/8.1. If I could direct Your Honours' attention to the ELMO image. Mr. Usher, I'd like you not to take General Krstic's face but the individual who is over the shoulder of General Krstic. And could you put that alongside Prosecutor's Exhibit 8/1, those two faces next to one another.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Colonel Kingori, do you see the individual in Prosecutor's Exhibit 58, which is the still photograph taken from the film, and do you see the man in the background of that? Is that the same man you saw with General Krstic on the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he is. This is the same person.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Usher, I've concluded with that set of exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Colonel Kingori, do you have in front of you a copy of the transcript of General Mladic's interview, which is marked in the upper right-hand corner as Prosecutor's Exhibit 79A.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, I'd like you to -- I'm going to read parts of this interview, and I'd like your observations and comments about each of the parts that I read to you. The first sentence -- for the record, I'm referring to Prosecutor's Exhibit 79A, and the first paragraph with "RM" I would like to start with the second complete sentence, or a portion of the second sentence, starting with "Our army." Let me read this portion of the interview. "Our army did not want to target either the civilian population or UNPROFOR." Now, Colonel Kingori, you lived in Potocari throughout the period of the takeover. What comments or observations do you have about General Mladic's comment about "Our army did not want to target either the civilian population or UNPROFOR"?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to draw you back to what I said on Friday concerning where BSA were targeting. They were mainly concentrating their fire power on Srebrenica village and Potocari. This is where mainly there were civilian population, heavy civilian population were in Potocari and Srebrenica. So seeing that they were not targeting the civilians, here I would not like to believe him. Concerning UNPROFOR, this is not correct because they were targeting the DutchBat -- the Dutch Battalion, their OPs, that is, their observation posts. They hit their OPs. They also surrounded one of the OPs, took some of the soldiers with them, and these cannot be called -- you know, that they were not targeting UNPROFOR. They definitely were. On one occasion, they also hit the Potocari DutchBat compound with their artillery shells, which is on record that we went there and analysed. So definitely the DutchBat compound was a safe area or somewhere that these guys were not supposed to have hit, but they did, knowing that this is a UN compound. So definitely they were targeting UNPROFOR and also civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me direct you to the remaining part of that sentence, which says: "We have provided transport, food, water, and medicine," referring to the civilian population. Do you have any comments or observations on that particular part of the sentence?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can say, on the side of transport, they provided transport for those people to leave the enclave -- okay, not for them to leave the enclave but to transport them to where they wanted to take them. For food, there was no food that they gave the civilian population, or even us, those who were inside that enclave. So there was no food. Water, there was a time we requested Major Nikolic, that was on the 12th, to provide water for the civilians because we didn't have enough water, and he brought one tanker of water. Now, for medicine, there was no provision of medicine. Okay. We can say that they treated some wounded people in Bratunac Hospital, the ones we took there, they accepted them and treated them, but there was no provision of medicine for the other people who were with us in Potocari. Those who were inside the compound or those who were outside the compound, they did not treat them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention to the following sentence: "In the course of the day, in the first round, we'll be evacuating women, children, the elderly, and all of those who want, of their own free will, without any coercion, to leave this combat area." What are your comments, Colonel Kingori, on that part of this sentence by General Mladic that people could leave of their own free will without any coercion?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: One thing to note here is that these people, that is, the Muslims, were not given a choice whether to leave or to continue staying in Srebrenica. After the enclave fell, they were just told, "We're providing transport to take you out," and that was it. They were not even asked where they want to be taken. So something to do with them leaving out of their own free will, that does not arise, because even us, we asked the BSA where they wanted to take these civilians because they did not indicate that they have a choice, and they told us they want to take them to Tuzla, for the Muslims to join their brothers who are Muslims in that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Colonel Kingori, do you have a copy of Prosecutor's Exhibit 67A, a transcript of the interview with General Krstic? Do you have that in front of you?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention to two sentences, and I'm going to ask you to do the same thing, to comment on the substance of these two sentences in General Krstic's statement. The first is the second to last sentence in the first paragraph: "We guarantee safety to civilians." Do you have any comments about that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: For one, I don't know what he's actually referring to because the safety of civilians was breached a long time before he made this comment. It started with the shelling of the enclave. That's when their safety was breached. That's when they were no longer safe anywhere in that enclave. And after that, when they went to DutchBat compound, they were still not safe because shelling was still going on, the BSA soldiers could still come in. Those who were outside the DutchBat compound were still not safe. The men had been herded in one area, one building, where there was so many of them inside that building they were stepping on each other, sleeping on each other and all that. And definitely that -- you cannot call that safety. They were not safe at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me turn to the second sentence in that first paragraph, and I quote: "They will be taken safely to a destination of their choice." Your comments, please, Colonel Kingori.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, as to the destination of their choice, these people, as I said earlier, were not asked where they want to go. They did not have a choice of their destination. So they were actually relying on where these BSA would take them. Whether it is to a good place, a bad place, or whatever, it all depended on the BSA. So they did not have a choice of where they wanted to go. On the side of safely, you know, being taken safely, well, that is something which is, to me, not very clear because they were transported, that is true, but as we had later, much later, they were not -- most of them did not reach their destination. So we cannot say that they were taken safely to where they wanted to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me know focus on the issue of choice of the refugees either to remain in Srebrenica enclave or to go to a destination of their choice. Did you, on the 13th of July, have an occasion to leave Potocari and go into Srebrenica, to the town of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could you tell the Judges what you observed when a Muslim woman did express their choice to remain in the town of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, on that day, that is, the 13th, we went to Srebrenica for patrol, with MSF personnel. Me, I was representing the UNMOs, and on the roadside, as we approached Srebrenica, we could see dead bodies on the roadside, next to buildings, and all that, all the way up to the Srebrenica town itself. Inside there, we went to the hospital, where we found some six old women, and we told them there that we wanted to go with them to Potocari, for their own safety, and also for them to be checked medically, but one of the women said that she does not want to leave Srebrenica. She resisted. She said she cannot. Unfortunately, one of the BSA soldiers confronted us and said we've got to go with that woman, that woman has got to leave, otherwise they are going to shoot her. So we told her the same thing, and, you know, she did not accept to leave, until we had to force her, physically lift her up, I personally did that, lift her up, put her in our vehicle, and took her down to Srebrenica town -- I mean Potocari DutchBat compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Finally, Colonel Kingori, based on your observations of General Krstic and the other high-ranking officers who were present in Potocari before, during the transportation of the Muslim civilians out of the enclave, did it appear to you that they were working together to achieve the goal of transporting all of the refugees out of the enclave?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly they were all working together, for the same cause, just to ensure that all the Muslims leave that place, all of them board those buses and go outside that enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I've concluded my examination of Colonel Kingori. Thank you, Colonel Kingori.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Harmon. Mr. Petrusic -- Colonel Kingori, you will now be asked some questions by Counsel Petrusic, who represents the defendant General Krstic. You have the floor, Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours; good morning, my learned friends.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Colonel. The other five officers, UN UNMOs in the enclave, arrived at the same time you did?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And other UNMOs, did they have contacts with Muslim either/or Serb officers during their stay there apart from of you, I mean, and independently of you?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were. We were all working together, but at times they could contact them in my absence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did they submit some reports independently of you, after their contacts with representatives of the Muslims -- that is, Serb side?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not true because any report that was being made from outside, whatever observations the UNMO made outside, they had to bring them together, we'd compile now as a team, and transmit it. So I knew almost everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Colonel Kingori, the commander of the Muslim army in Srebrenica was Nasir Oric, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were told there was a Nasir Oric, who I personally never met.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And the chief of staff was Ramiz Becirovic, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And the military organisation, headed by Oric with Becirovic as the chief of staff, was that military organisation the 28th Division?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, we had the 28th Division, but the way it was organised was not the same way a conventional army is organised, or the way orders are taken -- orders are given, executed, and also feedback given, it was not the same way as we had with the BSA.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You mean the whole setup was different in the army of Bosnian Muslims in the area of Srebrenica? The organisation was different.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is not what I mean, because any military organisation is different from the other. But I mean for the proper functioning of a military organisation, there are definite components and ways of executing their laws that is definitely followed. That did not seem to be there with the BSA -- with the BiH, as it was with the BSA.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: But the army of Bosnian Muslims in Srebrenica, it had the commander, the chief of staff, and their assistants. Would it not be part of their organisational layout?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that we can call that an organisation because, for one, to have an organised army or armed forces, at least the basic component has got to be the personnel and their arms. These people did not have the personnel, that is, the soldiers, as far as we knew. They also did not have arms. All their heavy weapons were in the DutchBat compound; all their machine-guns were also there. So maybe what could have been outside was small arms. But, I mean, what can an army with just rifles be doing? And that is why I'm saying that that was not an organised army. The BiH was not an organised army as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In view of the relief of the territory, that is, that area around Srebrenica is a mountainous area, there were infantry units because it was even impossible to position heavy weapons in that area, in view of the mountainous terrain.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, heavy weapons such as artillery is better positioned when it's behind hills, where it cannot be observed by the enemy or where it is difficult for the enemy to target it, and because it is a high trajectory, it can hit the enemy on the other side of the hills, so it doesn't matter whether there are hills or not. The artillery could be there if they wished to have them, or rather should have been there as a component of the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Colonel Kingori, members of the BSA, with their liaison officers, Major Nikolic and Major Vukovic, did you hear them complain of helicopters flying into the area during your stay in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, there was one time that we were told in a meeting in Bratunac by Colonel Vukovic that a helicopter had been heard flying into the enclave, and it was shot down by the BSA. And it was -- as he said, it was coming in support of the Muslims but they shot it down. That is one instance that we had concerning a helicopter. And when we asked him where the occupants of the helicopter went to, he did not give us an answer. And then after that, when we went to the BiH site, we asked them if they knew of any helicopter that had entered the enclave. They also denied having seen any helicopter. They also denied that a helicopter had crashed. But later on we gathered information from the locals that a helicopter had actually crashed inside the enclave and that some of the injured people were the chief of staff, that is, Ramiz, and later on in later meetings we could see he was limping, he was injured in the legs. So it's true it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Colonel Kingori, during your testimony on Friday, you said that in early June a meeting had been organised, and you mentioned it today, at the Bratunac Hotel, and that meeting was attended by Major Nikolic, Colonel Vukovic, and another high-ranking officer, whose face was shown you on the ELMO in Prosecutor's Exhibit 28/4. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And that third officer, did he rank higher than Nikolic and Vukovic, or didn't he?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That officer was -- as far as we thought, was slightly higher or above Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did the three of them come from the same formation in the Bosnian Serb army?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: With that, I'm not very sure, but I know there were two formations around the Srebrenica enclave, and they could have come from either or both of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us which were those two formations?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know there was the Drina Corps and the other one. I can't remember the actual names, but I have them on record somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: These other persons, were they also from the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they were. I think they were, but for record purposes, I'm not really sure whether they were from the Drina Corps or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Colonel Kingori, in your conversations with Vukovic and Nikolic, did you ever learn who had appointed them as liaison officers with you, or rather with the UN military observers in general?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were never told who appointed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You don't know to whom they were responsible in respect of that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there was the normal BSA hierarchy. Since they all belonged to the Bosnian Serb army, Major Nikolic was a lower person, we had Vukovic, we had Krstic, Acamovic, and all that, all the way up to General Ratko Mladic's level. So there were other stages which I definitely cannot be able to tell who was filling which post, but at least they were all in that setup of the BSA service.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: During that meeting, you said that Vukovic had made a proposal for a safe passage for the evacuation of Muslims towards Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, may I show this to Colonel Kingori. This is his statement, the statement that he gave to the Prosecutors of this Tribunal on the 23rd, 24th, 25th of September, 1997.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exhibit D10.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Colonel Kingori, this is your statement, is it not?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: On page 4, third paragraph from the bottom, you say: "Again he reiterated the offer to open a safe passage to evacuate the Muslims towards Tuzla."

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: On the basis of that, you concluded, Colonel Kingori, that there had been a plan concerning the events that would take place in July.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Colonel Kingori, could you now perhaps tell us what were other elements of this plan that may have been discussed at the meeting, and on the basis of which you reached your conclusion? Was there anything else in addition to what you have stated in this statement?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is very clear from this statement, if you can read the whole of it, the whole paragraph, that is, the third paragraph from the bottom, that in one of the areas, that is, the second line, where I say -- no, the third one: "During the dinner, Colonel Vukovic insisted on trying to find out what would be the reaction of the UN in case the BSA would capture the enclave and expel the population." What this means is that the something they had really discussed, something he was trying to pass on to us so that we could also take it on to the Muslims, that they are or they might take the enclave, they might capture the enclave. You can say the way I've written it there. By capturing the enclave, they are not saying that the Muslims are free to live inside the enclave. In fact, he said they would capture the enclave and expel the population. The population here, as far as I can understand, does not mean the BiH soldiers, it literally means all the people living inside that enclave. So if he later on thought of creating a safe passage, it meant they just -- he would clear a way for them to leave, you know, just in case they want to leave -- not in case they want to leave, just in case they have to. He would clear a safe passage for them to go to Tuzla, but of course he did not expect these people to just leave what was theirs, that is, the enclave. And because he did not expect them to leave that way, he knew there would be some resistance, and that is why he had earlier said that he would -- he wanted to know what the UN would do in case they attacked that enclave. So this is something which was preconceived, something they had thought of, maybe even planned, and they were just telling us to pass it on to the Muslims so that they are not blamed for the repercussions. That's how I concluded it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Colonel Kingori, the conclusion that you have just exposed is different from the conclusion made in the statement you gave to the Prosecutor, that is, this conclusion here is far broader. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't agree. These are similar conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Colonel Kingori, you will agree with me that on the 16th [sic] of July, 250 shells fell on Srebrenica. Is that a correct piece of information?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In the course of the following days, after the 6th, the shelling of the town continued; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In your reports, the number you give was between 50 and 100 shells, sometimes even more than that.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember stating that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: The damage caused to the structures in the town of Srebrenica, if we bear in mind the number of shells that fell --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petrusic, I'm sorry to interrupt you. Mr. Harmon, I don't know if you're going to mention the date. Mr. Petrusic, I think that you spoke about the 16th of July, but perhaps you were actually -- you actually wanted to say the 6th of July and not the 16th.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I was speaking about the 6th of July. There may have been an error in interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, the transcript will have to be rectified. The date in question is not the 16th of July but the 6th of July. Thank you very much for paying attention to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Colonel Kingori, if we bear in mind the number of shells that fell, the damage that was caused in the town of Srebrenica is somewhat out of proportion. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, there were casualties amongst the Muslim civilian population. The number you give is six wounded persons in the town. My question is very similar to the previous one: In view of the number of shells, the number of wounded persons is also out of proportion, however unfortunate it was.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On this issue of the number of shells and the number of casualties, we had even remarked somewhere, I know it is somewhere written in this document, that considering the number of shells that landed there, we were lucky to have very few casualties. All there is is that the shells were landing, luckily, if I can call it, on the roads, in the market, somewhere where luckily there are no buildings or there weren't many people there. But where we suspected they thought, that is, the BSA, where they thought there would be people. We're talking about the marketplace, the roads, inside the town of Srebrenica itself, and also the route from Srebrenica to Potocari, and all that, they were targeting those areas. So as I can say, it was just by luck that the damage was that minimal, comparing the number of shells. We are the ones who were counting them, and we could verify that, and we're sure that is the -- the number of shells we have indicated are the same. Concerning the injured, it was not just the injured, there were some who died. It's also on record here.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Colonel Kingori, in your statement given to the OTP, on page 6, the penultimate sentence, the second one from the bottom, states as follows: "I did not understand why they were targeting the town in this way. The only explanation was to harass the population, to bring them to flee."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: For the record, and to assist the witness, that is found on page 6, it is the second paragraph from the bottom, the large paragraph, and the statement referred to by counsel is in the middle of that particular paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, counsel. I'm reading from the Serbian translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petrusic, I'm very sorry to have to interrupt you again, but due to some exceptional circumstances, we have to stop at 10.45. Maybe we should do so before Colonel Kingori gives his answer, because if we let him answer your question, we will be way above that time. So please I should like to have a 20-minute break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petrusic, you can continue now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And so Colonel Kingori, before the break, we were talking about the statement that you made to the Prosecutor's Office and your conclusion that you did not understand why they were shelling the town in this manner, and your conclusion was that the only purpose of this exercise was to intimidate the population, to force them to flee. And this conclusion figured in your report to your superiors, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It did. This one did, but at the same time, it's also on record somewhere in these documents that they were aiming at the populated areas, and definitely the populated areas, you don't just aim there for any other purpose other than for hitting those people who are there, the inhabitants. On the same page, if you can see the second paragraph, where it starts with "The 8th of July," you can see I've said, "Shelling continued on populated areas as targets." This clearly means that they were targeting the populated areas, not just to harass, because you don't aim a gun at someone just to harass or intimidate, but also to kill. You know, the shell, when it lands somewhere, it does not discriminate whether -- I mean, all it does, it can kill, it can kill, although it could intimidate, but it also kills.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Colonel Kingori, in attachment 18 to your statement, you once again draw the same conclusion when it comes to the shelling of the Potocari base, and you say that it was quite evident that they were going off the mark, off the target, that is, off the building, on purpose. Is that true? Page 8 of the English version, third paragraph from below.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't get the actual place.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In the English version, page 8, one, two, three, the fourth paragraph from below, and the last sentence of that paragraph, the paragraph beginning with the words "The document attached, number 16 ..." Colonel Kingori, would it be easier if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps it would be simpler if you gave us the paragraph, you say the fourth from below, on page 8, perhaps you could tell us how the paragraph begins. It will be easier to identify it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. It begins with the words "They were obviously deliberately missing the buildings."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because even I can't find that passage. I was saying the paragraph begins with -- the paragraph begins how? Is it "The document attached number 16 is incomplete because ..." is that it, and after that, it would be one, two, three, four, five, the sixth line --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel Kingori, have you found it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Yes. Proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now, if you can read the preceding lines, and especially the second sentence on the same paragraph, where it starts "It mentions that from 1845 to 2051, 45 shells over flew the compound," by this I mean the Dutch Battalion compound, "causing a lot of panic among the refugees." So if you can relate that to the sentence that you're talking about, "They obviously were deliberately missing the buildings," I'm talking about the buildings in the DutchBat compound. That is the reference I have. That is the reference I'm using, that they were deliberately missing the UNPROFOR -- the DutchBat headquarters, and that is where the shells were over flying. In other words, if they wanted to hit it, they could have gotten it, definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Colonel Kingori, you knew Emir Suljajic, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. He was our interpreter from the BiH side.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And he only worked as an interpreter.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was our interpreter, one of them, because there were two.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Colonel Kingori, did Emir Suljajic tell you that between 1250 and 1350 in Srebrenica there were 49 shells recorded?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Likewise, the two shells fell in the vicinity of the hospital.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. He told us that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Could then one infer that it was on the basis of his information that you reported to your command about those 49 shells, or rather two shells barely missing the hospital?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reason why we used this information was that we could not be able to go to that --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Mr. President. If I may, and I should also like to apologise to the witness, whether the information was used in order to notify the higher command, that is, I should like to receive a brief answer without any explanations.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President and Your Honours, I would request that the witness be permitted to provide explanations if explanations clarify his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petrusic, could you repeat your question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did Colonel Kingori use the information he received from Emir Suljajic to send it on to the higher command in his report?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So Colonel Kingori, will you answer this question truthfully, truthfully. But we shall hear the answer of the witness, Mr. Petrusic. Colonel Kingori, yes.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, on this occasion what happened was that we were unable to go for patrols. We were unable to go to Srebrenica itself to see what was going on. So as our own initiative, because we wanted to know what was happening, we decided to send one of our interpreters who, after some discussion with him on how he's going to get to that place, that is, Srebrenica, investigate what is going on, report to us using the radio set that we had given him, and then we used that information. The point here was that we were unable to go there. Secondly, even in the sitrep that we sent to the UN headquarters, we said -- we actually wrote the word "NCBU", to mean "not confirmed by UNMOs". It is evident it is there, something we have not clarified, we have not confirmed ourselves. We had to indicate. So it was not meant for any other purpose other than to update us on what is going on. But we could not clarify, we could not confirm, and we reported it that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question, Colonel Kingori, is whether the information obtained in this manner was then communicated to your superiors.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was, but with the words "NCBU," not confirmed by UNMOs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Petrusic, does that answer satisfy you?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, thank you. I have only a few questions more, and I hope you will bear with me and I hope the witness will bear with me too.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Colonel Kingori, did you see General Krstic arrive in Potocari on the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: When was that, approximately?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember the actual timing, but it was somewhere in the middle of the day, somewhere there. I'm not very sure of the actual timing, but he came together with Major Nikolic and the other senior officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: In your testimony on Friday, you said that Krstic issued orders to soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I said, and I can remember very well, was that when we were together with General Mladic and the other officers, some of the senior officers, including Krstic, would go out to their soldiers, I could see them going to their soldiers who were lined up by the side of the road or in buildings or somewhere, who were around there, and he would talk to them. And immediately you could see them dispatch or go somewhere, or something like that; that means, obviously, he was giving orders to them. Not just him alone, but other people like Colonel Vukovic and all that, they would still go there, give orders, and then come back. So I saw that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Colonel Kingori, in view of an organisational layout, or rather hierarchial order in the army, and it is if not identical then very similar in all the armies of the world, would you think from that point of view, would you think it normal for a high-ranking officer, that is, a General, yet in the presence of lower ranking officers, would you think it natural and logical for him to issue orders to the troops?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was happening in this case was a bit different from the normal, because even in normal circumstances someone of General Mladic's level could not issue orders to the soldiers, but he was. So they were doing it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us how long did General Krstic stay in that particular area?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I cannot tell for sure, but at least I know we were together for quite some time, not in the same location but at least he was in that vicinity for quite some time. Let's say over an hour, it was something like that, but I did not know where he went after that. But the following day he was still around. That means that he was somewhere there, even if he left, maybe he just went and came back to continue with his work.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Colonel Kingori, you reported to your command about the presence of the Bosnian Serb army officers in Potocari, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Did you also report the presence of General Krstic there?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I did not. Same with other senior officers, I did not report about every senior officer that was there. There were so many.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: But the rule was to notify the superior command about the presence of officers; would that be correct to say?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can say you could have reported, but then you would not be able to report on every senior officer who was there. It was impossible, considering the circumstances that we were in, and also considering that we were doing a lot of things at least together for these refugees. Also to cope, and we were just two observers, to cope with the refugees, cope with the military situation in that area, cope with the food situation, water, and all those things. We could not have been able to concentrate on each and every senior officer there.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: And did you report about the presence of Mladic?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You also reported about the presence of Vukovic.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: Likewise, you reported about the presence of Colonel Acamovic, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You also reported about the presence of Major Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Nikolic at least was with us throughout.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: You mentioned a number of higher ranking officers therefore. You said that they were present on the location. The only officer whose presence you did not report to your command was General Krstic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct. I believe that there were other senior officers who we did not report on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this concludes my cross-examination of this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Petrusic. Mr. Harmon, do you have any additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have no additional questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Harmon. Judge Fouad Riad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good morning, Colonel Kingori.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I have been listening very carefully to your very thorough testimony, and still I would like to ask you a few questions to see things clearer. In one of your -- in one of the films you have just seen concerning, in particular, General Krstic with a journalist, he said -- it is Exhibit 67. He mentioned at the end, "We are not afraid of airstrikes. We are going all the way." Now, what did he mean by "We are going all the way"?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the interpretation to that is that he meant he's going to ensure the enclave is free of all Muslims, to get rid of all the Muslims from the enclave, and that is the way that he meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Because I'm just putting this together with another declaration by Colonel Vukovic. I think you said that in a meeting, when you had the meeting with the high-grade officers, he mentioned that Muslims should leave the enclave in their totality, if not they would be all killed. Do you think these two statements are coherent? I mean, was the one confirming what the other one was saying, to leave or be killed?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, that confirms what the earlier statement was all about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And in your opinion, who was higher in grade, Vukovic or General Krstic? Was he a General at the time?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know him as a General. I knew him as a Colonel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You did not know him as a General. He was a Colonel too.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was a Colonel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: The Defence counsel was mentioning that a General cannot give orders to soldiers. In relation to what was happening, soldiers doing all that you mentioned, including stealing your glasses and stealing civilians and your own people, United Nations people, was any action taken to stop this?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the only action I can remember was concerning my sunglasses. Nothing else was being done to stop whatever was going on inside that enclave, and especially in Potocari. No senior officer tried to stop it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But you brought always complaints about what was happening. I mean, of course your sunglasses are precious to you, but other lives were also involved. But did you always bring complaints to the higher authorities among the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was always doing that, but nothing was being done about the whole thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Yes. And the answer of the Defence counsel, he said, "Because Generals cannot give orders to soldiers." Were these soldiers more or less undisciplined, they would do everything, or was there a real discipline in the army and they could receive orders from their superiors?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, these soldiers could receive orders from their superiors. It's only that they were not following, that is, they were not -- I don't know what I can say, whether they were not obeying. But the senior officers could give the officers, we could see them telling them to do something extra or to go to a certain place, and they could go. But concerning this particular issue of the atrocities or doing something bad to the civilians or to us, no one was telling them to stop it. I could not hear anyone telling them that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good. So I would like to have a very precise conclusion. There was a firm command, if I understood you rightly, a firm chain of command, I remember your words, which means that a General can give orders to his, let us say, to the people who are lower in grade, and so on, until they reach the soldiers, and in between this chain there was nothing irregular. I mean, each one could be obeyed by his superior.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: A real army.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: A real army. It was a real organised army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You just mentioned that not only that it was -- that they were highly equipped with tanks and with heavy military weapons and so on. Were the Muslims equally equipped?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Muslims did not have anything as compared to what the BSA had. They did not have tanks, they did not have artillery, they did not have mortars, they did not have machine-guns. In fact, during my whole stay there, I saw only one machine-gun belonging to the BiH. And that as compared to what the BSA had, it was nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Did the Muslims have inside Srebrenica, did they have hidden weapons? You mentioned, for instance, that the hospital was hit and missed three times by a few metres. Was the hospital used to hide weapons, for instance? That's why they were trying to target it. They targeted, you said, civilians. Were civilians used as a shield to hide weapons?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, as far as I know, and I inspected that hospital, there were no soldiers there and there was no military base or headquarters or an ammo depot, or something like that, inside that hospital. There was none at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You mentioned that they were shelling the civilians not only to force them to flee but also to have casualties. Did I understand that rightly?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's true, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: All right. And in the event where they were, in fact, forcing them to flee, were they able to flee?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, they could not be able to flee because they were being bombarded from all sides. There was no escape route, there was no where that they could have gone through to go to wherever. So they were actually all forced to one area, towards Potocari.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: They were forced to what area?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Towards Potocari. Even those that were -- not on the western side, those who were in the eastern side, the Sudisuta [phoen] village and all that, they were all forced to come to Srebrenica, and I testified that they all left to Potocari. So they were channelled to one area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But I conclude from what you said that it was not to let them free --

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not to let them free, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: It was to destroyed.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: My main concern and what I could get from all that shelling was to cause maximum casualties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And, of course, you brought that up to your superiors.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I did that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And nothing happened.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Something that was planned, that is, for the airstrikes to hit the military target for the BSA, but the airstrikes did not produce much. In fact, the only thing that they managed to hit was one tank, and I think one -- and I think one bridge or something like that. One tank, and it's on record here somewhere, I don't know whether it was a bridge or artillery piece. I'm not very sure, but that was the only thing they managed to hit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Who are "they"?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The NATO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: But then they could not continue.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They could not continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Was that to save you?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In fact, at that time the reason they did not continue was to save the whole enclave. Because the BSA called us for a meeting and they said, if the airstrikes continue, if they continue, they are going to finish the whole enclave. They said that. So we had no choice but to tell the UN whatever was happening. And also one thing to remember there is that immediately, just before the airstrikes, we were called for a meeting by the BSA, which we were not allowed to go, as I had said earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were not allowed to attend just because the UN feared that we might be taken as human shields against the airstrikes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: So you were in danger, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were in danger ourselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You were in real danger.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And you explained that in the meetings with the high-grade officials, the high-grade officers, of the -- Vukovic and the other ones whom you met?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I did that. We explained to them but they were always assuring us that they don't have anything against UNPROFOR, they've got nothing against us at all. All they wanted was the Muslims. But then when a shell lands somewhere where you are, it does not discriminate whether you are Muslim, whether you are UNMO, or whether you are UNPROFOR. It can hit and kill you all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And you felt that in the meetings with these officers, they were all one -- one opinion, or did somebody prove some opposition? For instance, when Colonel Vukovic would tell you, "If the Muslims do not leave, they will all be killed." I think there were other officers including -- I don't know the other names. Was General Krstic with them?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time he was not there. I did not notice him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: You did not notice him?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not notice him. But no other senior officer ever opposed whatever was said, like that meeting when he said he was going to kill all of them, no one opposed it, no one talked against it at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: No one. You mentioned that on the 12th of July you noticed the arrival of new Serb soldiers who were different from other BSA soldiers. In what way were they different? And do you think they were from other parts than Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, these soldiers who came first wore black, as compared to the normal camouflage, green camouflage, that we were used to on the BSA side. You know, BSA could have the normal camouflage that is green, also blue for, I think, the police. But then these guys were in black, and we believed they were from Arkan's Brigade, which was part of the brigades in that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: It's from that area --

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were from Arkan's. We suspected from they were from Arkan's Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: And Arkan's Brigade came from Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Arkan's Brigade, as far as I knew, was headquartered somewhere in Erdut. That was in eastern Slavonia. That was where it was headquartered. And it was very feared, it included masonries, people from other countries who could go to fight and then be paid for it or something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Paid for by whom?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paid for by the guys they were fighting for. Like, in this case, it should have been the Bosnian Serbs who were paying for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you, Colonel Kingori.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Riad. Judge Wald.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Colonel Kingori, I have only basically one question. The Prosecutor's Exhibit 67, the film clip of the journalist's interview with General Krstic, he makes the following statement: "The Drina Corps has been conducting this operation successfully. We have not suspended this operation. We are going all the way to liberate the municipality of Srebrenica. We guarantee safety to civilians. They will be taken safely to a destination of their choice." Now, this statement was made at Potocari in July 12th. You were there at the time, as I understand. Not at the interview, but you were in Potocari on the 12th and other days. In reading that statement in light of what you saw during the period you were in Potocari, do you interpret that statement to mean that the Drina Corps is conducting this operation, not just the takeover of Srebrenica, but the evacuation operation which is guaranteeing safety to civilians, according to General Krstic, to a destination of their choice? In short, the Drina Corps was in charge of the whole operation. And would that be consistent with what you observed while you were there?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, what this meant was that they're going to clean the whole of that enclave of the Muslims, ensure that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: "That enclave" now meaning Potocari as well as Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The whole enclave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The whole enclave, to make sure -- of course, they were using the more known villages, that is, Srebrenica and Potocari, but they meant the whole enclave, that it would be free of Muslims and that would be the successful finishing of their job. The only problem I have there is with the free -- to be taken to the place of their choice. That did not happen and that actually was not the case because they were not asked where they wanted to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: No, I understand that part of your prior testimony, Major, but I just want to ask one question over again to make sure I have your answer, and that is: It was your impression, consistent with what General Krstic said, that the Drina Corps was in charge of not only cleaning out the enclaves, making sure that the Muslims, but the evacuation and what happened to the people, whatever happened to them, that they were taking charge of that whole operation.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, they were taking full responsibility of all that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE WALD
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Judge Wald. Colonel Kingori, I have only two questions for you. You testified at some point, in response to a question that was put to you by Mr. Harmon, that Serbs had been the aggressor in that case. Could you now tell us what was the result or conclusion of your observations on the basis of which you could state that?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this was based on basically what the Muslims had, comparing what the Muslims had, and what the Bosnian Serbs had, and also the activities which were going on at that particular time. It meant that it was the Muslims who are receiving, from the BSA, than actually what was going out from the Muslim side. In fact, we did not record anything going out from the Muslim side. That means if it is the Serbs, the Bosnian Serbs, who were actually directing their fire against the Muslims, it meant obviously they were the -- they -- what can I call it? They were the aggressors, they were the aggressors, as far as we knew. And also for the start of this fight in the enclave, they are the ones who started, they are the ones who started hitting the enclave. It was not the other way around. That means that they are the ones who started it, and therefore they remained the aggressors, as far as we could guess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My second question is the following: In order to ask this question, I should need assistance of the technical room. I need Exhibits, Prosecution Exhibits 79A, first of all, and then after that one, 67A. I shall like to ask you, Colonel Kingori, to watch carefully the bodyguards of General Mladic on that footage and also to have a look at the bodyguards of General Krstic, if it is possible. And after that I'm going to ask my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think this will be enough for the purpose of my question. If you can please stop here and show us the next exhibit, that is, 67A.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is actually Exhibit 66, because it is only the video clip that we need here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I'm sorry. Could we see it now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. Okay. Very well. My question for you, Colonel Kingori, is the following: Do you see any link, any connection, between the bodyguards of General Mladic and bodyguards of General Krstic? I do not wish to lead you in your answer. Perhaps you can answer my question the way it has been put to you. Do you think there is any connection, any link, between the two? Do you think that we are talking about the same persons, or are they different persons?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't understand whether you mean whether they are the same person, that is, General Krstic and General Mladic, or what do you mean? Because these are two different people altogether.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your conclusion, therefore, is that they were bodyguards. I have another question for you. Were you present when General Mladic was being interviewed and when General Krstic was being interviewed as well? Were you present at those two occasions?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was present when General Mladic was being interviewed, but when Krstic was being interviewed, I was not there. But I'm sure I was just somewhere around there, but I did not witness it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question was the following, actually: This blonde soldier who seemed to be a bodyguard of General Mladic, was he the same as the one who was with General Krstic?

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was not very observant on that, so I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's okay. You have answered my questions. Thank you very much, Colonel Kingori. I don't think we have any more questions for you. Thank you very much for coming here to testify before the International Criminal Tribunal. We know that you spent some very difficult moments there in the area. Thank you very much for coming and we wish you a safe journey home. But before we let you go, I think that we have to check on the status of certain exhibits. Mr. Dubuisson or Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would move for admission into evidence the following Prosecutor's Exhibits: Prosecutor's Exhibit 28/1, 28/3.2, 28/8.1; Prosecutor's Exhibit 5/3B; Prosecutor's Exhibit 58; Prosecutor's Exhibit 66; 67A and B, which are transcripts from the video of the interview with General Krstic; Prosecutor's Exhibit 76, which is the film clip where Colonel Kingori has identified an individual who attempted to steal his sunglasses; Prosecutor's Exhibit 75; Prosecutor's Exhibit 77, which are United Nations military observer reports and UNPROFOR reports. There are 37 such reports in the binder. Prosecutor's Exhibit 78, which is a film clip of Bosnian Serb soldiers handing out candy; Prosecutor's Exhibit 79 and 79A and B, the interview of General Mladic and the transcripts relating thereto. I believe, if I'm correct, that should conclude all of the exhibits that the Prosecutor has tendered through this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petrusic, do you have any objections or remarks concerning these exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, just one thing that I should like to check. The exhibit that was shown on your request, 66A, is that the video clip of the interview given by General Krstic? Has that been tendered into evidence by the Prosecution? Is that the Exhibit 66 that we are talking about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, 66 is the video clip and 66A and B are the transcripts that relate to the video clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence does not object to the exhibits tendered by the Prosecution, save for the Exhibit 66 and for the following reason: Until today the Defence has not been able to check the locality, the specific location where the material was filmed. As regards all of the remaining exhibits, we do not have any objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Harmon, as regards the exhibit in question, do you wish to say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I do. This witness has viewed the video, he was present in Potocari, he has identified a relevant building that's in the background as being in Potocari, in addition to which we will present additional evidence from Mr. Ruez, who will be able to identify the exact location in Potocari where the interview of General Krstic occurred. But I think it's sufficient for purposes of introduction of this exhibit that this witness has identified the exhibit as having been filmed in Potocari, and from the context of the statement that is -- 67A clearly supports the time and probably the location where this film was taken. But more directly, as I say, this witness has specifically identified the location where the interview in Potocari took place. So we would move to admit 66, the film clip, at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Petrusic, your objection needs some explanation for the Chamber. Do you object to the authenticity of the document, or if there is another purpose in your objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the authenticity of the document and the interview given by General Krstic is not objected to by the Defence. However, so far we have not been able to ascertain the particular location of the interview, because in the background of the video clip there is something which we cannot precisely identify. We cannot identify the structures that were referred to by Mr. Ruez here before the Chamber. Colonel Kingori, if I may paraphrase his answer, stated that it was somewhere outside Potocari, if I was careful enough following his testimony, if I'm correct in quoting him. So for these reasons the Defence will have to adopt a position on this particular exhibit, we will have to make a representation on that, and so far, as I have already stated, we have not been able to verify the location.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. Petrusic. You may sit down. I think that Colonel Kingori was not -- did not agree to your quotation. The witness is still here, so let me ask the question once again. Colonel Kingori, as regards this particular video clip, do you have anything else to add? You remember the exhibit in question is Exhibit 66, that is, the interview given by General Krstic.

utterances.speaker: JOSEPH KINGORI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I remember this particular clip, and even when I was answering, I said it was somewhere in Potocari, not outside Potocari.
